## Goal

Give CI some coverage of the full-screen interface. Today it has none: the workflow builds `tui.c`/`tuifmt.c` and runs the formatter unit tests, but nothing ever launches `sst -t`, so the curses layer itself is only ever exercised by hand.

## Blocked by

ISSUE_TTY — while piping into `sst -t` hangs, every non-interactive invocation is a CI hang rather than a test.

## Suggested approach

Two levels, either or both:

1. **Cheap, no pty.** Once the non-tty fallback lands, assert that `sst -t` with piped input falls back to plain mode, plays, and exits 0. This needs no extra tooling and would have caught the hang.
2. **Real pty via tmux.** Drive an actual full-screen session and assert on captured panes — the quadrant/status panels render, a command updates them, the terminal is restored on exit. AGENTS.md documents the recipe (`tmux new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 …`, `send-keys`, `capture-pane`).

Level 2 is the more valuable coverage and the more flake-prone: it depends on sleeps and timing. If you take it, make the waits condition-based (poll `capture-pane` until the expected text appears, with a bounded overall timeout) rather than fixed `sleep`s, and keep it out of the critical path if it proves unstable. `tmux` is available on GitHub's Ubuntu and macOS runners but should not be assumed — install or skip explicitly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] CI exercises `-t` in some form on at least Linux.
- [ ] No fixed-`sleep`-based races: 20 consecutive runs pass.
- [ ] Failures produce useful diagnostics (captured pane content), not just a timeout.
- [ ] Bounded by a CTest `TIMEOUT` so a hang fails fast instead of burning the job budget.

## Notes

Never redirect the game's stdout inside a tmux session — it breaks curses rendering. See AGENTS.md.

## Goal

Clear the existing compiler warnings, then make new ones fail the build.

A fresh Release configure with `-Wall -Wextra` currently produces **33 warnings**:

```sh
cmake -S . -B /tmp/wchk -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-Wall -Wextra"
cmake --build /tmp/wchk 2>&1 | grep -c 'warning:'
# 33
```

They fall into a few families:

- `-Wunused-result` on unchecked `fgets`/`scanf`-style calls — concentrated in `setup.c`, with a few in `finish.c`, `osx.c`, and `sst.c`. Note this overlaps with the unchecked-`fgets` EOF bug tracked separately; fixing that one properly removes some of these.
- `-Wsign-compare` in `sst.c` (`helpme`).
- Switch fallthroughs in `battle.c`, `finish.c`, and `reports.c` — some are intentional (there is at least one `// no break` comment), so these need reading rather than blanket suppression.

## Why it matters

CI deliberately does **not** use `-Werror` today, precisely because `main` would fail immediately. Until that is fixed, a genuinely new warning introduced by a change is invisible in the noise.

## Suggested approach

Two phases, ideally two PRs:

1. Fix the warnings. Handle the unchecked returns for real rather than casting them to `(void)`; mark deliberate fallthroughs explicitly so intent is recorded in the code.
2. Add `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` to the build (or to the CI configure step) once the count is zero.

Watch the compiler difference between platforms: the Release warning set is larger than Debug's because of `_FORTIFY_SOURCE`, and Clang on macOS will not produce an identical list to GCC on Linux. Whatever gate is added must be green on all four CI legs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `-Wall -Wextra` produces zero warnings in both Debug and Release.
- [ ] Deliberate fallthroughs are explicitly marked, not silenced wholesale.
- [ ] `-Werror` (or equivalent) is enforced in CI and green on Linux and macOS.
- [ ] No behaviour change: `ctest --test-dir build` stays green, and plain mode stays byte-identical.

## Notes

Best done after the EOF-handling fix, so the unchecked-input warnings are resolved by real fixes rather than by silencing.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

## Problem

The README documents a Windows build that cannot work:

> Then run the command "cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c"

Two things break it:

1. **`main.c` is a dead hello-world stub.** It is tracked in the repo but referenced nowhere in `CMakeLists.txt`, so it plays no part in the real build — but `*.c` sweeps it into the MSVC command line, where its `main()` collides with the one in `sst.c`.
2. **`tui.c` needs curses.** It includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and MSVC has no such header. `sst.c`, `finish.c`, and `osx.c` all reference `tui_*` symbols, so it cannot simply be dropped from the file list either.

Point 1 predates the TUI work; point 2 arrived with it. The README does now note that full-screen mode is Unix-only, but the build command itself is still wrong.

## Two ways to resolve

**Make it true** — stub the TUI out on Windows (`#ifdef WINDOWS`, with `tui_init()` returning FALSE so the game always runs in plain mode), delete `main.c`, and verify the documented `cl` command actually produces a working `sst.exe`.

**Or make the docs true** — delete `main.c` regardless, and rewrite the Windows section to describe a build that works (explicit file list excluding `tui.c`, plus whatever stubs that needs) or to state plainly that Windows is currently unsupported.

Either is fine; the current state — documented instructions that fail — is the thing to fix. Deleting `main.c` is worth doing on its own merits in both cases.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `main.c` is gone (or is genuinely part of a build).
- [ ] The README's Windows section matches reality — the documented command works, or the limitation is stated.
- [ ] The Unix build is untouched: CMake builds Debug and Release, `ctest --test-dir build` green on Linux and macOS.

## Notes

Nobody appears to have a Windows toolchain in play right now, so "make the docs true" is the lower-risk option unless someone can actually test MSVC. Adding Windows to the CI matrix would be the way to keep it honest afterwards.

content.text:
Right now, nothing enforces it — it's convention. The `@AGENTS.md` import works, but a rule added directly to CLAUDE.md would be silently honored, and you'd have two sources of truth again.

**The specific ways this will drift**, in rough order of likelihood:

The `#` shortcut is the big one. Pressing `#` in a Claude Code session appends the new rule to CLAUDE.md — it's a one-keystroke action whose entire purpose is writing rules, and it doesn't know AGENTS.md exists. Right behind it are the CLAUDE.md-targeting skills: both `revise-claude-md` and `claude-md-improver` edit CLAUDE.md by name, and earlier today `revise-claude-md` did exactly that — it put the TUI section into CLAUDE.md, which is why the restructure had to move it afterward. `/init` would rewrite the file wholesale and clobber the pointer entirely. And any agent or human can reasonably add "just one rule" to a file literally named CLAUDE.md.

There's also a quieter failure: if AGENTS.md is ever renamed or deleted, `@AGENTS.md` resolves to nothing and Claude silently loses every rule. No error, no warning — just an empty ruleset.

**Three ways to fix it, and what each actually buys:**

A **CI check** is the only thing that genuinely makes sure. Assert that CLAUDE.md contains nothing beyond its pointer, that the `@AGENTS.md` line is present, and that AGENTS.md exists and is non-trivial. That catches every vector above on the next PR, including `#`. Best implemented as a CTest test rather than inline workflow shell — same reasoning as `journey.sh`: it then runs locally too, and CI is just the thing that runs `ctest`.

**Stating the prohibition in the file** costs one line and steers well-behaved agents before they write. CLAUDE.md currently *describes* where rules live but doesn't *instruct* anyone not to add them there. A line like "Do not add rules to this file — edit AGENTS.md instead" converts a description into a directive. AGENTS.md already covers the reverse direction ("keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing"). This won't stop `#`, which doesn't read the file first.

**Symlinking CLAUDE.md → AGENTS.md** is the most elegant in principle: one file, and anything writing to CLAUDE.md — including `#` — writes through to AGENTS.md. I'd avoid it here, though. Windows checkouts without `core.symlinks` turn the symlink into a text file containing the string `AGENTS.md`, which would silently give a Windows contributor no instructions at all. This repo already claims Windows support it doesn't have; I wouldn't add a second Windows-shaped trap.

My recommendation is the check plus the directive line — the line steers agents, the check guarantees it. Worth knowing: with that combination, `#` still writes to CLAUDE.md and gets caught at PR time rather than prevented, so the check's failure message should say where to move the content.

One coverage note while we're here: Codex, Cursor, and Copilot's coding agent all read a root AGENTS.md natively, so they're already correct. Only Copilot's older IDE completions would need a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` pointer — and if you add one, the same check should cover it too.

content.text:
**No — it works on Linux and macOS, but breaks on Windows by default.** I tested each case rather than reasoning about it.

Git itself stores the symlink correctly: mode `120000`, with the blob content being the literal string `AGENTS.md`. A normal Unix clone materializes a real symlink and reads through fine. But cloning with `core.symlinks=false` — which is **Git for Windows' default**, since the installer's "Enable symbolic links" checkbox is off unless you tick it — produces a regular 9-byte text file whose entire content is the word `AGENTS.md`. A Windows contributor's agent then reads a CLAUDE.md containing no rules and gets no error. Silent, total loss of instructions. Even with `core.symlinks=true`, Windows additionally requires Developer Mode or admin rights to create symlinks at checkout.

Two more findings worth knowing, both OS-independent:

**Atomic saves destroy the link.** `sed -i` — representative of the write-temp-then-rename pattern many editors and tools use — replaced the symlink with a regular file copy, and the change never reached AGENTS.md. That's a worse failure than the pointer approach, because afterward both files look perfectly plausible while silently diverging.

**Claude Code refuses to write through symlinks outright.** My Edit tool rejected it: *"Refusing to write through symlink… Resolve the symlink and pass the real target path explicitly."* So the main benefit you'd hope for — `#` and agent edits transparently landing in AGENTS.md — doesn't materialize for agent edits at all. Plain shell appends (`>>`) do write through correctly, and `git archive`/zip export preserves the symlink, so those two are fine.

There's also a trap in combining approaches: a CI check running on Linux would clone with symlinks intact and report everything healthy, while the Windows contributor silently has nothing. CI cannot detect that failure mode at all.

**My recommendation is to stay with the pointer file.** It degrades gracefully everywhere: on every OS it's a real text file that at minimum tells a human where the rules live, and Claude Code's `@AGENTS.md` import resolves it. This repo also still aspires to Windows support — that's issue #15 — so adding a second Windows-shaped trap seems like the wrong direction.

The honest cost of that choice: `#` will keep writing to CLAUDE.md, and the pointer approach can only *detect* that at PR time, not prevent it. That's what the CI check buys you, and it's why the check's failure message should name AGENTS.md as the place to move the content.

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
#
# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
# truth that slowly disagree.
#
# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
# an agent session with no rules at all.
#
# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"

# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Any
# real body of rules blows past this.
MAXBYTES=600
# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
MINAGENTS=2000

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
fi
if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
fi
if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')

# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
fi
if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
fi

# CLAUDE.md points at it and holds nothing else.
if ! grep -q '^@AGENTS.md[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE"; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has no '@AGENTS.md' import line -- Claude Code would not load the shared rules"
fi
if [ "$claudebytes" -gt "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is $claudebytes bytes, over the $MAXBYTES limit -- rules belong in AGENTS.md, not here"
fi

# Rules arrive as list items or new sections. The pointer needs neither,
# so their presence below the title means content landed in the wrong file.
if tail -n +2 "$CLAUDE" | grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md contains headings or list items below the title -- move that content to AGENTS.md"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	printf 'AGENTS.md is the source of truth for every coding agent; CLAUDE.md only imports it.\n' >&2
	printf 'Put project rules in AGENTS.md and leave CLAUDE.md as the pointer.\n' >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'instructions OK (CLAUDE.md %s bytes, AGENTS.md %s bytes)\n' "$claudebytes" "$agentsbytes"

Implemented and under verification. What it does:

The check lives in `tests/instructions.sh`, registered with CTest as `instructions` — so it runs on `ctest --test-dir build` locally and on all four CI legs, same pattern as the journey test. It guards both directions: CLAUDE.md must stay a pointer (import line present, ≤600 bytes, ≤4 non-blank lines, no headings or list items below the title), and AGENTS.md must stay substantial (≥2000 bytes, still has its `## Development workflow` section) — because the `@AGENTS.md` import fails *silently* if that file is renamed or emptied, which is the failure mode with no error message at all.

I falsified it against seven drift scenarios before wiring it in: a `#`-style bullet append, an added rules section, a `/init`-style wholesale rewrite, AGENTS.md deleted, the import line removed, AGENTS.md gutted to a stub, and a rule added as plain prose. The prose case initially **passed** — a real gap, since bullets and headings were the only shapes I was matching. That's what the line budget closes: CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so 4 non-blank lines is the exact current count rather than a generous ceiling, and any smuggled line trips it.

CLAUDE.md also now carries the directive itself — "Do not add rules here — edit AGENTS.md instead" — so a well-behaved agent is steered before it writes, and the check catches the ones that aren't.

Every failure message names AGENTS.md as the destination, and the line-budget message distinguishes the two cases: move the rule, or update the constant if you genuinely reworded the pointer.

The verifier is checking portability and, more usefully, trying to find drift the check still misses — plus a second opinion on whether pinning to exactly 4 lines is too brittle for ordinary rewrapping. ui-review I'm skipping deliberately: there's no user-facing game behavior in this change. Bullet append, added section, `/init`-style wholesale rewrite, AGENTS.md deleted, import line removed, AGENTS.md gutted, and one-line prose rule: **7/7 fail**, each with the actionable message you intended (the `/init` case trips three checks at once, which reads well). Baseline repo passes.

I hunted for realistic drift the check misses. Three classes slip through:

1. **Rules folded into an existing prose line** (no new line). Appending `… Always run ctest before pushing and never commit to main:` to the existing sentence → 4 lines, 226 bytes → **passes**. A whole rule paragraph folded in the same way (334 bytes) also **passes**. The byte cap is the only backstop here and it currently leaves ~430 bytes of headroom above the real 168. Tightening `MAXBYTES` toward ~300 would shrink the hiding space considerably at no cost to legitimate rewording. This is the most plausible miss of the three, though I'd note the natural agent behavior (`#` shortcut, "add a rule to CLAUDE.md") produces a *new* line, which you do catch.
2. **A second import line.** Replacing the prose with `Rules live in AGENTS.md; also see the extra project rules below:` + `@RULES.md`, keeping 4 lines → **passes** (100 bytes). A one-line guard — fail if any `^@` line other than `@AGENTS.md` exists — closes it exactly.
3. **Rules in other files Claude Code actually loads** — this is the biggest surface, since the script only ever looks at `$ROOT/CLAUDE.md`:

Every construct is POSIX and BSD-safe; I exercised the script under `dash` and `busybox ash` (both pass) and behind a BSD-style padding `wc` shim (passes — the `| tr -d ' '` is doing its job here as in journey.sh):
- `wc -c < f | tr -d ' '` ✓ · `grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$'` ✓ (combined flags are POSIX; the exit-1-on-zero-count quirk is harmless with no `set -e`) · `grep -q` BRE with `[[:space:]]` ✓ · `grep -qE` with `(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])` ✓ (leading `-` inside the bracket is literal and portable) · `tail -n +2` ✓ (POSIX, supported by BSD tail) · `-lt`/`-gt` ✓ · `printf` ✓ · `${1:-.}` under `set -u` ✓.
- One cosmetic nit: `'^@AGENTS.md[[:space:]]*$'` leaves `.` unescaped, so `@AGENTSxmd` would also match. Zero practical impact; escape it if you care.

Passes from `/`, from an unrelated scratch dir, with a relative argument from the repo root, with **no** argument (defaults to `.`), and with a repo path **containing spaces** (quoting is correct throughout). It creates no files and no temp dirs — `git status` is unchanged after runs, and there is nothing to clean up, which is a nice property versus journey.sh.

### `MAXLINES=4` brittleness — my second opinion

**It is brittle, but the brittleness is the feature, and I'd keep it.** Measured sensitivity by re-wrapping the *identical* sentence at several widths:

| wrap width | prose lines | non-blank | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 / 80 / 72 cols | 2 | 4 | PASS |
| 60 / 50 cols | 3 | 5 | **FAIL** |

So ordinary reformatting is safe as long as it stays at ≥72 columns — which matches this repo's prevailing style (AGENTS.md, README, and the scripts all wrap around 72). Narrowing the wrap, or rewording into a third line, trips it. That is acceptable because: the failure is loud, deterministic, arrives in CI rather than silently, and the message explicitly says *"if you reworded the pointer, update MAXLINES in this script"* — which is exactly the right instruction. And the trade-off is unavoidable: catching a one-line prose rule (your scenario 7) *requires* an exact line budget; any slack you add to accommodate rewrapping is slack a rule can hide in. The one thing I'd suggest is a brief note in the script (or AGENTS.md) that the pointer is wrapped at 72 columns by convention, so a future formatter run has a documented target.

None. No `actionlint` needed here; nothing macOS-specific was untestable this round beyond the shim-based simulation described above.

input.content:
test: keep AGENTS.md the single source of agent instructions

AGENTS.md holds the rules and CLAUDE.md only imports it, but nothing
enforced that. Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: the `#`
shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites it wholesale, and tools that
target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them know AGENTS.md
exists, so the result is two sources of truth that slowly disagree.

The check runs under ctest, so it guards local runs and all four CI
legs. CLAUDE.md must keep its @AGENTS.md import, import nothing else,
and stay within a byte and line budget with no headings or list items
-- the shapes rules arrive in. AGENTS.md must stay substantial and keep
its workflow section, because the import fails silently if that file is
renamed or emptied, leaving a session with no rules and no error. No
other CLAUDE*.md may exist anywhere, since Claude Code loads those from
subdirectories too.

A personal CLAUDE.local.md at the root is exempt: failing someone's
local ctest over private preferences would be user-hostile. It is now
gitignored, which is what keeps that exemption from becoming a way to
commit shared rules.

The budgets are deliberately tight rather than generous. Headroom is
where a rule hides, and matching whole import tokens keeps a rename
artifact like @AGENTS.md.bak from reading as the allowed import.

`AGENTS.md` holds the project rules and `CLAUDE.md` only imports it — but nothing enforced that. This adds a check, registered with CTest so it guards local `ctest` runs and all four CI legs.

Rules drift into `CLAUDE.md` easily and silently. Claude Code's `#` shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and tools that target `CLAUDE.md` by name edit it directly. None of them know `AGENTS.md` exists.

## What it checks

- `CLAUDE.md` keeps its `@AGENTS.md` import, imports **nothing else**, and stays within a byte and line budget with no headings or list items — the shapes rules arrive in.
- `AGENTS.md` stays substantial and keeps its workflow section. This matters because the `@AGENTS.md` import fails **silently** if that file is renamed or emptied: a session with no rules and no error.
- No other `CLAUDE*.md` exists anywhere (matched case-insensitively, since macOS filesystems are case-insensitive by default and a lone `claude.md` would load there). Claude Code loads these from subdirectories and `.claude/` too, so any of them would be a second shared source of truth.

A personal `CLAUDE.local.md` at the root is exempt — failing a developer's local `ctest` over private preferences would be user-hostile — and it's now gitignored, which is what stops that exemption from becoming a way to commit shared rules.

`CLAUDE.md` also now states the rule itself ("Do not add rules here — edit AGENTS.md instead"), so a well-behaved agent is steered before it writes and the check catches the ones that aren't.

## Design notes

The budgets are deliberately tight rather than generous: headroom is where a rule hides. The line budget is the *exact* current count, because catching a rule added as plain prose requires it — any slack is slack a rule fits in. The failure message says to update the constant if the pointer was genuinely reworded.

Import matching blanks **whole tokens** only. Both refinements there are load-bearing, not belt-and-braces: matching only at line starts missed `... see @RULES.md.` (four lines, 183 bytes, and a functional second import), and matching partial tokens let a rename artifact like `@AGENTS.md.bak` read as the allowed import.

## Test plan

Developed against an adversarial corpus and falsified throughout — a bullet append, an added section, an `/init`-style rewrite, a deleted or gutted `AGENTS.md`, a removed import, a prose rule, a folded rule, a second import both mid-line and on its own line, the six-form prefix family, subdirectory and `.claude/` copies, and case variants all fail with actionable messages. Legitimate content passes: the real repo, a root `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/agents/*.md`, real build trees, sentence punctuation after the import, and paths containing spaces.

`shellcheck -s sh` clean; runs under dash and busybox ash; `ctest` 3/3 in Debug and Release.

Two constructs can only be validated by the macOS legs here: `find`'s `-iname`/`-ipath` and BSD `sed -E`. Both fail loudly rather than silently — a divergence makes the baseline repo fail on the first run — so the CI checks on this PR are sufficient validation.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

**Next up: #5 — `sst -t` hangs when stdin or stdout is not a terminal.**

It's the right one for three reasons: it's a confirmed bug rather than a nice-to-have (piping into `-t` exits 124 after hanging, and with `TERM` unset it dies with a raw ncurses error); it's the only issue blocking another, since #13 can't add TUI coverage to CI while every non-interactive invocation hangs; and the fix is small and self-contained — an `isatty` check in `tui_init` reusing the fallback path that already exists for undersized terminals.

Natural sequence after it: **#6** (the EOF reprompt loop) is the same class of problem in adjacent code, and fixing it properly also clears some of the unchecked-`fgets` warnings that #14 needs gone before `-Werror`. Then **#13** becomes unblocked, and **#7 → #11** gets the panels behaving before colour lands on them.

input.message:
New change to review as an expert in games and CLI games. Branch fix/tui-requires-tty, created from main at e93b2d1. This fixes issue #5. All uncommitted:

The bug: `sst -t` started curses unconditionally, so with no terminal it hung. Confirmed before the fix — piped stdin with TERM=dumb exited 124 after hanging; with TERM unset it died with "ncurses: cannot initialize terminal type"; and even with TERM=xterm, redirecting stdout hung.

The fix:
1. osx.c — new `stdio_is_terminal()` returning `isatty(STDIN_FILENO) && isatty(STDOUT_FILENO)`. It lives there because <unistd.h> cannot meet sst.h: sst.h declares `void pause(int)`, which collides with POSIX `pause(void)`. osx.c already includes <unistd.h> and does not include sst.h.
2. tui.h — declares it.
3. tui.c — `tui_init()` returns FALSE before `initscr()` when there is no terminal.
4. sst.c — the existing fallback now distinguishes the two reasons: "Full-screen mode needs a terminal -- using the classic display." vs the pre-existing "Terminal too small for full-screen mode (need 72x24)."
5. tests/journey.sh — now accepts extra arguments after the build type and passes them to the game.
6. CMakeLists.txt — new ctest test `journey-tui` running the SAME journey with `-t` and ENVIRONMENT TERM=dumb. The idea is that falling back to plain mode means the output must be identical, including the existing assertion that no escape sequences appear.

I confirmed the test fails for the right reason before the fix (`game exited with status 124`) and passes after. All three original repro cases now exit 0; the interactive TUI still renders correctly under tmux and exits 0; plain mode is unchanged; the too-small-terminal path still gets its own message at 60x20.

Please review the player-facing behaviour: is falling back silently-but-with-a-notice the right call, or should a player who explicitly asked for -t get something more prominent (or a non-zero exit) when they cannot have it? Is the wording right, and does it read well in the flow of the game's startup? Are there terminal situations I have not considered where this either wrongly falls back (a player who genuinely has a terminal but gets denied) or wrongly proceeds — e.g. stdin a tty but stdout a pipe, `script`/`expect` wrappers, running under a terminal multiplexer, an ssh session without a pty, or a valid tty with an unusable TERM (note: with a real tty and a bad TERM, initscr() still exits the process; I deliberately scoped that out — tell me if you think that is wrong). Also: is testing the -t path by asserting it produces byte-identical plain-mode output a sound approach from a player's perspective, or does it risk locking in behaviour we would not want? Read-only: report findings with severity and a verdict, do not edit files.

content.text:
Issue #5 is fixed and under review. The change in short:

**The bug:** `sst -t` called `initscr()` unconditionally. With no terminal that either hung forever or killed the process with a raw ncurses error. I reproduced all three variants first, including one I hadn't tested when writing the issue — even with a valid `TERM`, redirecting stdout hangs.

**The fix** is small: a new `stdio_is_terminal()` in `osx.c`, and `tui_init()` returns FALSE before touching curses when there's no terminal, reusing the fallback path that already existed for undersized terminals. The helper lives in `osx.c` specifically because `<unistd.h>` can't meet `sst.h` — the `void pause(int)` vs POSIX `pause(void)` collision the issue warned about. The fallback message now distinguishes the two reasons, so "no terminal" and "terminal too small" don't say the same misleading thing.

**The test is the part I like most.** Rather than a bespoke fallback test, `journey-tui` runs the *exact same journey* with `-t` under `TERM=dumb`. If falling back to plain mode works, the output must be identical — and the journey already asserts zero escape sequences, which proves it's genuinely plain mode rather than curses drawing something plausible. TDD held: it failed with `game exited with status 124` before the fix, passes after.

Verified: all four ctest tests pass, all three repro cases exit 0, the interactive TUI still renders correctly under tmux and exits 0, plain mode is unchanged, and a 60x20 terminal still gets its own too-small message.

I deliberately scoped out one adjacent case and flagged it for review: a *real* tty with an unusable `TERM` still lets `initscr()` exit the process, since handling that means switching to `newterm()`.

<result># Review: `fix/tui-requires-tty` (issue #5)

## Verdict

The fix is correct, minimal, and lands the right player-facing behaviour for the case it targets: `sst -t` with no terminal now plays the classic game instead of hanging or dying. I verified all three original repro cases exit 0, that the new `journey-tui` test genuinely fails without the guard (status 124 with `TERM=dumb`, status 1 with `TERM` unset), and that the interactive TUI, the too-small-terminal path, and plain mode are all unaffected. Falling back with a notice — rather than erroring out — is the right call for a game, and the `&&` in `isatty(stdin) && isatty(stdout)` makes it robustly conservative. However, I think scoping out the "real tty, unusable TERM" case is the wrong call: on a real terminal with an unknown `TERM` the game still exits 1 with a raw ncurses message and no game, and on a real pty with `TERM=dumb` (Emacs `M-x shell`) it starts curses and renders a single unusable border line while swallowing all input — both are the same player experience issue #5 is about, and both are closable with the same non-fatal ncurses probe. I'd merge this, then immediately follow with that. Approve with should-fix items.

## Answers to your specific questions

**Silent-ish fallback vs. something louder / non-zero exit.** Falling back is right. A non-zero exit would mean "you asked for the fancy display, so you get no game" — which is precisely the failure mode of the bug. The notice is adequate for the piped/CI case. The one place it genuinely fails to reach the player is `sst -t > file` from a real terminal: the reason the fallback happened is that stdout isn't a terminal, so printing the reason *to stdout* puts it in the file where the player can't see it. I confirmed this — the player types blind and the notice ends up as line 1 of `file`. That specific message belongs on stderr. The journey script captures `2>&1`, so the test is unaffected either way.

**Wording and flow.** "the classic display" is well chosen — it matches both `README.md` ("the game uses its classic scrolling display") and `sst.doc` ("classic scrolling display remains the default"), so it isn't inventing terminology. The `--` matches the game's house style. It reads fine sitting above the ASCII Enterprise banner. My one wording complaint is that the two branches are now inconsistent in what they tell the player: the new one says what happens next, the older one doesn't. See should-fix 3.

**Is the byte-identical-output test approach sound?** The approach is sound, and it's sound partly *because* the implementation doesn't actually do what the comment claims. `journey-tui` re-runs the same assertion set; it does not diff the two captures. A literal byte-diff would be wrong and flaky here — `randomize()` seeds from `time(NULL)`, so every run has a different galaxy, stardate, and Klingon count. And the two runs legitimately differ by exactly one line (the fallback notice). So assertion-parity plus the no-escape-sequences check is the right level of strictness: it pins "the player gets a complete, correct, escape-free classic game" without locking in output we might want to change. Does it risk locking in behaviour we wouldn't want? Only mildly: it asserts that a fallback happens at all, which is the intent. What it does *not* pin is that the player is told why — see should-fix 2. Two comments overstate what's enforced; see minor 5.

**Terminal situations.** I worked through the ones you listed on real ptys:

| Situation | Behaviour | Right? |
|---|---|---|
| tmux / screen | TUI renders correctly, exit 0 | yes (verified) |
| ssh with pty | TUI (same as tmux) | yes |
| ssh without pty, cron, `docker run` without `-it` | falls back, exit 0 | yes |
| stdin tty, stdout redirected (`sst -t > f`) | falls back, complete game in the file, exit 0 | yes — notice invisible to player (nit 7) |
| stdin redirected, stdout tty (`sst -t < moves.txt`) | falls back | defensible; you lose panels for a scripted playback, but that's niche |
| `script -qec './build/sst -t' /dev/null` with piped stdin | TUI starts (real pty), then hangs at end of input (exit 124) | correct behaviour, but see minor 6 |
| **real pty, `TERM=dumb`** (Emacs `M-x shell`) | **curses starts, one border line, no prompt, input ignored** | **no — should-fix 1** |
| **real tty, unknown/unset `TERM`** | **`ncurses: cannot initialize terminal type ($TERM="nosuchterm"); exiting`, exit 1** | **no — should-fix 1** |

## Findings

**Should-fix 1 — "real terminal, unusable TERM" is the same bug, and the fix is three lines.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c`, `tui_init()`. Two reachable cases survive:

- Real pty + `TERM=nosuchterm` (or `TERM` unset under `env -i`, a serial console, a typo'd export): `initscr()` calls `exit()` from inside the library. The player asked to play Star Trek and got `ncurses: cannot initialize terminal type` and exit 1 — no banner, no game, no hint that dropping `-t` would work.
- Real pty + `TERM=dumb`: `isatty` is true so curses starts, but `dumb` has no `cup` capability, so only `+- Quadrant ----+- Status ---+` ever reaches the screen. The message window never appears, typed input produces nothing, and the game looks hung. This is Emacs `M-x shell`, which is a mainstream way for a developer to run a CLI game.

Both are closable with the same non-fatal probe. I verified the API behaves as needed:

```
TERM=xterm      setupterm rc=0  cup=present
TERM=dumb       setupterm rc=0  cup=ABSENT
TERM=nosuchterm setupterm rc=-1        (returns ERR, does NOT exit)
TERM unset      setupterm rc=-1        (returns ERR, does NOT exit)
```

So in `tui_init()`, before `initscr()`: `int err; if (setupterm(NULL, STDOUT_FILENO, &err) == ERR) return FALSE;` and reject when `tigetstr("cup")` is `NULL` or `(char *)-1` (needs `<term.h>`). Both fall into the existing fallback with a suitable message. I'd argue this belongs in *this* branch — it is the same one-sentence bug ("`-t` must never leave the player without a game"), and leaving it out means issue #5 gets closed while the more embarrassing variant (a hard crash on a real terminal) stays open.

**Should-fix 2 — nothing asserts the player is told why the fallback happened.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/journey.sh` has no `want` for the notice, so `journey-tui` passes just as happily if the `prout()` in `sst.c` is deleted and the game silently ignores `-t`. Since journey.sh already takes the pass-through args, the script can tell it is in `-t` mode. Add `want "fallback notice missing" "using the classic display"` guarded on the `-t` case (or unconditionally in a dedicated tiny test). That is the assertion that makes this a behaviour test rather than a crash test.

**Should-fix 3 — the two fallback messages disagree about whether they tell the player what happens next.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c`:

```
Full-screen mode needs a terminal -- using the classic display.
Terminal too small for full-screen mode (need 72x24).
```

A player on a 60x20 terminal is told the problem but not the resolution, and then a full game starts anyway — mildly disorienting, and inconsistent now that its sibling sets a better precedent. Suggest `Terminal too small for full-screen mode (need 72x24) -- using the classic display.` (I confirmed at 60x20 this still renders on one line with room to spare.)

**Should-fix 4 — the docs don't mention the fallback.** `README.md` says "It needs a terminal of at least 72x24" and `sst.doc` (line ~1535) describes `-t`, but neither says what happens when you can't have it. This branch exists because a user hit exactly that gap. One sentence in both: "If the terminal is too small, or the game is not attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with no tty), `-t` prints a notice and uses the classic display." Cheap, and it is the place the player looks before filing issue #5 again.

**Minor 5 — two comments claim strictness the test doesn't have.** `tests/journey.sh` says "the output has to come out identical, escape sequences and all", and your summary says "the output must be identical". The test asserts assertion-parity, not identity — and identity is impossible anyway (random galaxy; plus the extra notice line). The comment will mislead the next person into "fixing" the test by adding a diff. Reword to what it really guarantees: same journey, same assertions, exit 0, no escape bytes.

**Minor 6 — the `TERM=dumb` environment on `journey-tui` no longer pins anything.** With no tty the `isatty` check short-circuits before `TERM` is ever consulted, so `TERM=dumb`, `TERM=xterm`, and unset are now identical paths. It's still a good historical pin (I confirmed the un-fixed build fails at 124 under `dumb` and at 1 under unset), so keep it — but note that if you take should-fix 1, `TERM=dumb` becomes meaningful again in a *different* place (capability probing), and you'd want a second case to keep both pinned. Also worth recording somewhere: `script(1)` cannot be used to add real TUI coverage to CI, because the pty keeps the game blocked on `wgetnstr` after piped input is exhausted (I measured exit 124). A TUI CI test needs an expect-style driver or a tmux harness.

**Minor 7 — the notice goes to stdout, which is the one stream we just established isn't the player's.** `sst.c`. For the `sst -t > file` case the message lands in the file. `fprintf(stderr, ...)` for the no-terminal branch specifically would reach the player; the journey captures `2>&1` so tests are unaffected. Slight tension with the AGENTS.md "all output through `prout`" rule, which is why I'm calling it minor rather than should-fix.

**Minor 8 — `journey.sh`'s positional-then-passthrough argument handling silently misparses a natural invocation.** Running `./tests/journey.sh ./build/sst -t` (exactly what a developer reproducing issue #5 would type) consumes `-t` as `BUILD_TYPE`, never passes it to the game, and then fails with `FAIL: debug output leaked into a -t build` — a confusing message for a test that silently didn't test what was asked. I reproduced this. Validate `BUILD_TYPE` against `Debug|Release|RelWithDebInfo|MinSizeRel|""` and error out otherwise, or take a `--` separator. Also, `[ "$#" -ge 1 ] && shift` twice is a cryptic way to spell "drop up to two args"; a comment or `shift $(( $# < 2 ? $# : 2 ))` reads better.

**Nit 9 — no prototype cross-check for `stdio_is_terminal()`.** It's declared in `tui.h` and defined in `osx.c`, which includes neither `tui.h` nor `sst.h`, so a future signature change won't be caught by the compiler. The header comment explaining the `pause(int)` vs POSIX `pause(void)` collision is genuinely good and worth keeping; the placement is the right pragmatic call.

**Nit 10 — the Windows build path in `README.md` is broken (pre-existing, slightly aggravated).** `stdio_is_terminal()` sits inside `#ifndef WINDOWS` in `osx.c`, but `sst.c` calls it unguarded. `cl /DWINDOWS *.c` would now fail on that symbol in addition to already failing on `tui.c`'s `curses.h` (from PR #2). The README both documents the Windows build and notes the TUI isn't part of it; something has to give eventually.

**Observation (pre-existing, PR #2, but squarely in "the player asked for `-t`") — on a stock 80x24 terminal the TUI eats the player's first keystroke.** The message window is `LINES - 13 - 1` = 10 rows, while the startup banner is ~14 lines, so `sst -t` opens with `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]`. I reproduced it at exactly 80x24: typing `regular` at that moment yields `Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?egular` / `What is "egular"?`. Since 80x24 is the default size of most terminals, this is close to the median first-run experience of the feature. Not this branch's bug, but you're one line from the minimum supported size and it deserves its own issue.

## What I exercised

- Read the full branch diff (`osx.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `sst.c`, `tests/journey.sh`, `CMakeLists.txt`), plus `journey.sh` in full, `main()`'s argument loop, `tui_init()`, and `README.md` / `sst.doc` for the `-t` terminology.
- Built Debug and ran the whole suite: `tuifmt`, `journey`, `journey-tui`, `instructions` — 4/4 pass, 5.56 s.
- Reproduced all three original failure cases against the fixed binary: `TERM` unset, `TERM=dumb`, `TERM=xterm`, each with piped stdin — all exit 0, all print the fallback notice, all play a complete game.
- **Falsification:** copied the tree to a scratchpad, removed the `stdio_is_terminal()` guard from `tui_init()`, rebuilt, and ran the new test — fails with `game exited with status 124` under `TERM=dumb` and `status 1` under unset `TERM`. The test is a real regression guard.
- Real ptys via tmux: 100x30 interactive TUI (panels render, game plays); 80x24 (found the first-keystroke paging issue); 60x20 (too-small message, verified as a clean single line with `cat -A`); `TERM=dumb` on a pty (found the unusable single-border-line rendering, confirmed the process alive and ignoring input); `TERM=nosuchterm` on a pty (found the hard exit 1).
- stdin-tty/stdout-redirected inside tmux: drove a full game to the farewell line, confirmed exit 0 and that the notice lands in the file rather than on screen.
- `script -qec './build/sst -t' /dev/null` with piped stdin: confirmed the pty path starts curses (152 ESC bytes emitted) and then hangs at input exhaustion.
- Wrote a small `setupterm`/`tigetstr("cup")` probe to confirm the non-fatal alternative to `initscr()` behaves as needed across `xterm` / `dumb` / unknown / unset `TERM`.
- Reproduced the `journey.sh ./build/sst -t` argument misparse.
- `gh issue view 5` for the stated scope. No files modified (`git status` shows only your six).</result>

content.text: Confirmed exactly as described — at 80x24, the default size of most terminals, the banner triggers a paging prompt and `getch()` eats the first character: `What is "egular"?`. That's close to the median first-run experience of `-t`. Filing it, since it's out of scope here:

input.content:
## Problem

On an 80x24 terminal — the default size of most terminal emulators — `sst -t` opens with a paging prompt, and the first character the player types is swallowed.

Reproduce:

```sh
tmux new-session -d -x 80 -y 24 -s std './build/sst -t; sleep 10'
tmux capture-pane -t std -p | tail -3
#    THE USS ENTERPRISE --- NCC-1701
#  [HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]
tmux send-keys -t std 'regular' Enter
tmux capture-pane -t std -p | tail -3
#  Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?egular
#  What is "egular"?
```

The `r` is consumed by the `getch()` behind the paging prompt, so the game sees `egular` and rejects it. The player's very first interaction with full-screen mode is an error message.

## Why it happens

The message window is `LINES - PANELH - 1` rows — 10 on a 24-line terminal (`tui_pageheight()`, `tui.c`). The startup banner is about 14 lines, so `skip()` reaches the paging threshold before setup asks its first question.

At 100x30 there is no problem, which is why this was missed: the panels and the banner both fit.

## Why it matters

80x24 is the classic default. This is close to the median first-run experience of the `-t` flag, and it looks like the game is broken rather than merely paging.

## Suggested approach

Several options, worth weighing rather than picking blind:

- Don't page the startup banner at all — reset `linecount` after the banner, or suppress paging until the first real prompt.
- Give the message window more room by shrinking the panels, though `PANELH` is already the minimum that fits a 10-row grid plus borders.
- Have the paging prompt push back a character it did not mean to consume, or drain only a newline.
- Raise the minimum terminal size for `-t` above 24 lines, so the fallback handles it. Least appealing: it would deny the feature to standard terminals.

Whichever is chosen, the fix should be verified at exactly 80x24, not just at a comfortable size.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At 80x24, `sst -t` accepts the player's first answer without losing a character.
- [ ] No paging prompt appears before the game has asked anything.
- [ ] Paging still works normally later in the game, when output genuinely exceeds the window.
- [ ] Plain mode unaffected; `ctest --test-dir build` stays green.

## Notes

Pre-existing since the TUI landed (#2); found while reviewing the non-tty fallback (#5). Testing needs a pty — see AGENTS.md for the tmux recipe, and note that CI cannot currently cover the TUI (#13).

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

input.message:
New change to verify. Branch fix/tui-requires-tty, created from main at e93b2d1 (PR #16 merged, so main now has the instructions check). Fixes issue #5. All uncommitted; modified osx.c, tui.c, tui.h, sst.c, tests/journey.sh, CMakeLists.txt, README.md, sst.doc.

The bug: `sst -t` started curses unconditionally. Confirmed before the fix — piped stdin with TERM=dumb hung (exit 124); TERM unset died with "ncurses: cannot initialize terminal type" (exit 1); TERM=xterm with stdout redirected hung. ui-review then found two more, both on REAL ptys: TERM=nosuchterm exits 1 with no game, and TERM=dumb starts curses and renders one unusable border line while swallowing input (this is Emacs M-x shell). I reproduced all five.

The fix:
1. osx.c — new `stdio_is_terminal()`: `isatty(STDIN_FILENO) && isatty(STDOUT_FILENO)`. It lives there because <unistd.h> cannot meet sst.h (sst.h declares `void pause(int)`, colliding with POSIX `pause(void)`); osx.c already includes <unistd.h> and not sst.h.
2. tui.c — new `tui_terminal_capable()`: calls `setupterm(NULL, fileno(stdout), &err)`, which REPORTS an unusable TERM instead of exiting the way initscr does, then rejects terminals whose `tigetstr("cup")` is NULL or (char *)-1 (cannot address the cursor). Result cached in statics because main() asks again to word the notice. Needs <term.h>.
3. tui_init() checks both before initscr().
4. sst.c — three distinct fallback messages (no terminal / cannot do full-screen / too small), each now saying it will use the classic display. The too-small one is deliberately short (57 chars) because it only ever prints on a narrow terminal.
5. tests/journey.sh — accepts game args after the build type; validates the build-type argument (previously `journey.sh ./build/sst -t` silently misparsed -t as a build type); asserts the fallback notice appears when -t is passed.
6. CMakeLists.txt — new ctest test `journey-tui`: the same journey with `-t`, ENVIRONMENT TERM=dumb, TIMEOUT 120.
7. README.md and sst.doc document the fallback. sst.doc edited preserving CRLF.

Locally verified: TDD red/green (journey-tui failed with "game exited with status 124" before the fix); 4/4 ctest; all five repro cases now play a full game and exit 0; interactive TUI still renders at 100x30 and exits 0; too-small message fits one line at 60 columns; shellcheck/sh -n/dash -n clean; the notice assertion has teeth (I built a tree with the prout deleted and it failed).

Please verify: fresh Debug AND Release builds, and pay attention to whether `setupterm`/`tigetstr` link cleanly — they may live in libtinfo rather than libncurses on some systems, and CMakeLists only links ${CURSES_LIBRARIES}; if there is any chance this fails to link on the macOS runners or on a system with a split tinfo, say so, because that is a build break rather than a test failure. Also check <term.h> does not collide with anything (ncurses term.h defines lowercase macros for capability names such as `lines`, `columns`, `tab` — confirm none of our globals or locals are shadowed, in either build type). Then: ctest in both types; re-run the five repro cases; confirm the interactive TUI is unaffected under tmux at 100x30 and 80x24; confirm plain mode is byte-identical to main; check the journey.sh argument validation rejects bad input and accepts every legitimate form; confirm the new notice assertion cannot false-positive; and confirm the sst.doc edit kept CRLF endings and did not corrupt the file (the in-game `help` command reads it). Scope cleanup to paths you create. Report PASS/FAIL.

ui-review approved the fix but argued I'd scoped the issue too narrowly — and it was right. I verified both cases it found on real ptys before acting:

**`TERM=nosuchterm` exits 1 with no game** (a typo'd export, a serial console), and **`TERM=dumb` starts curses and draws one unusable border line** while swallowing all input — that's Emacs' `M-x shell`, a mainstream way to run a CLI game. Same one-sentence bug as #5: *`-t` must never leave the player without a game.* Closing #5 while the worse variant — a hard crash on a real terminal — stayed open would have been the wrong call.

The fix is `setupterm()`, which *reports* an unusable `TERM` instead of exiting the way `initscr()` does, plus a `tigetstr("cup")` check for terminals that can't address the cursor. Both bad-`TERM` cases now play a complete game and exit 0.

I also took the reviewer's other findings: the fallback notice is now **asserted** (previously the `prout` could be deleted and the test would still pass — I proved the assertion has teeth by building a tree with it removed), `journey.sh` now rejects the natural misinvocation `journey.sh ./build/sst -t` instead of silently misparsing `-t` as a build type, all three messages say what happens next, and the fallback is documented in README.md and sst.doc.

One thing I fixed that the review didn't catch: my new too-small message **wrapped at 60 columns** — precisely the width where it appears. It's now 57 characters and fits.

Both trees configure and build clean: **Debug 0 warnings, Release 17** — the unchanged pre-existing `-Wunused-result` set, nothing new from `tui.c` or `osx.c`.

`setupterm`/`tigetstr` do link, but I want to be precise about *why*, because your instinct was right that this is fragile:

- On this box (and on the `ubuntu-latest` runners, same Debian packaging) `setupterm`, `tigetstr` and even `cbreak` live in **libtinfo.so.6, not libncurses.so.6**. The link only succeeds because `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libncurses.so` is a **linker script** containing `INPUT(libncurses.so.6 -ltinfo)`, so `-lncurses` transitively drags in `-ltinfo`. The built binary's `DT_NEEDED` confirms both.
- I proved the dependency is real by linking the same objects against `-l:libncurses.so.6` (bypassing the script): **`undefined reference to symbol 'cbreak@@NCURSES6_TINFO_5.0.19991023'`**.
- **macOS: no risk.** Apple's ncurses is not split — `libncurses.dylib` carries the terminfo entry points, and `term.h` ships in the SDK. `find_package(Curses)` there resolves everything in one library.
- **Residual risk: a distro that splits tinfo without providing the linker script** would fail to link with the current `target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${CURSES_LIBRARIES} m)`. That is a build break, as you say, not a test failure. Neither CI platform is affected, so I am not calling it a blocker — but the one-line hardening is cheap if you want it, and CMake has already computed the answer during configure (`NCURSES_LDFLAGS:INTERNAL=-lncurses;-ltinfo` sits in the cache from pkg-config):

  ```cmake
  find_library(TINFO_LIBRARY tinfo)
  if(TINFO_LIBRARY)
    target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${TINFO_LIBRARY})
  endif()
  ```

New review request, separate from the TUI (#2), docs (#3), CI (#4) and instructions-check (#16) work you approved — all merged. Branch fix/tui-requires-tty from main at e93b2d1, fixing issue #5. All uncommitted: osx.c, tui.c, tui.h, sst.c, tests/journey.sh, CMakeLists.txt, README.md, sst.doc.

The bug: `sst -t` started curses unconditionally, so without a usable terminal the player got no game. Five confirmed variants — piped stdin with TERM=dumb hung (124); TERM unset died with "ncurses: cannot initialize terminal type" (1); TERM=xterm with stdout redirected hung; and on REAL ptys, TERM=nosuchterm exited 1 with no game while TERM=dumb started curses and drew one unusable border line while swallowing input (Emacs M-x shell). The last two were found by ui-review, which argued the issue was scoped too narrowly; I agreed and widened it rather than closing #5 with the worse variant open.

The fix:
1. osx.c — `stdio_is_terminal()`: `isatty(STDIN_FILENO) && isatty(STDOUT_FILENO)`. It is in osx.c because <unistd.h> cannot meet sst.h (sst.h's `void pause(int)` collides with POSIX `pause(void)`); osx.c already includes <unistd.h> and not sst.h.
2. tui.c — `tui_terminal_capable()`: `setupterm()` reports an unusable TERM instead of exiting the way initscr does, then `tigetstr("cup")` rejects terminals that cannot address the cursor. Cached in statics because main() asks again to word the notice. Requires <term.h>.
3. tui_init() checks both before initscr().
4. sst.c — three distinct notices (no terminal / cannot do full-screen / too small), each saying it will use the classic display. The too-small one is deliberately short (57 chars) because it only prints on a narrow terminal — my first wording wrapped at 60 columns, which is exactly where it appears.
5. tests/journey.sh — takes game args after the build type; validates the build-type argument (previously `journey.sh ./build/sst -t` silently misparsed `-t` as a build type and failed confusingly); asserts the fallback notice when `-t` is passed.
6. CMakeLists.txt — new ctest test `journey-tui` (same journey with `-t`, TERM=dumb, TIMEOUT 120); and an explicit `find_library(TINFO_LIBRARY tinfo)` link, because the verifier proved setupterm/tigetstr live in libtinfo on Debian/Ubuntu and only link today because libncurses.so is a linker script pulling in -ltinfo — luck rather than a contract.
7. README.md and sst.doc document the fallback (sst.doc edited preserving CRLF).

Verifier PASSED: Debug 0 warnings / Release 17 (unchanged pre-existing set); 4/4 ctest in both types, 20 journey runs no flakes; all five repro cases now play a full game and exit 0; interactive TUI unaffected at 100x30 and 80x24; plain mode proven BYTE-IDENTICAL to main using an LD_PRELOAD time shim so both binaries seed the same galaxy; <term.h>'s 477 lowercase capability macros intersected against every identifier in sst.h/tui.c/tuifmt.c — empty intersection; sst.doc CRLF intact and in-game `help` still works; the notice assertion proven to have teeth and to be specific to -t.

Two things I want your judgment on:
- The `getch()`-based paging prompt at 80x24 eats the player's first keystroke. Verified pre-existing (reproduces identically on main), so I filed it as #17 rather than fixing it here. Agree with that scoping?
- `stdio_is_terminal()` requires BOTH stdin and stdout to be ttys, so `sst -t < moves.txt` on a real terminal falls back rather than showing panels. ui-review called that defensible but niche. Is `&&` the right choice over checking only stdout?

Please review as an expert in C, curses/terminfo, CMake and POSIX shell: correctness of the terminfo probe (including whether `setupterm` before `initscr` is safe and whether the static caching is sound), the header-collision reasoning, the CMake linking change, the shell changes, and whether the three messages are right. Read-only; end with an explicit approve or request-changes verdict.

**`setupterm`/`tigetstr` live in `libtinfo`, not `libncurses`,** on Debian/Ubuntu. The build only links because `libncurses.so` is a *linker script* containing `INPUT(libncurses.so.6 -ltinfo)` — it proved the dependency is real by linking against `-l:libncurses.so.6` directly and getting `undefined reference to 'cbreak'`. Harmless today, since `journey-tui` always takes the no-terminal path — but it would have silently stopped matching if a future test exercised the size path. ### Verified independently

I reproduced the bug class rather than trusting the report. All five variants now play a full game and exit 0. On **real ptys** via tmux (the path none of the piped tests reach): TERM=dumb at 100x30 → `This terminal cannot do full-screen mode -- using the classic display.` followed by a normal game; TERM=nosuchterm → same, with **no** ncurses error text anywhere (the old "cannot initialize terminal type" is gone); xterm at 60x20 → `Terminal too small (need 72x24) -- using classic display.`, unwrapped on 60 columns (57 chars, confirmed in the pane capture); xterm at 100x30 → the Status panel still draws, which is the important safety result: `setupterm()` before `initscr()` does not break the good path.

### Findings (nits only)

1. `CMakeLists.txt:46-55` — `ENVIRONMENT "TERM=dumb"` does not select the code path the comment claims. Under ctest, stdin and stdout are pipes, so `stdio_is_terminal()` fails first and the terminfo probe is never reached: I ran `journey-tui` with TERM=dumb, TERM=xterm and TERM=nosuchterm and all three pass identically, and the notice captured under ctest conditions is "needs a terminal", not "cannot do full-screen mode". Net effect: `tui_terminal_capable()`, the heart of this fix, has **zero** automated coverage. Suggest either rewording the comment so it doesn't claim to pin the TERM=dumb case, or adding a pty test (tmux is already the documented technique in AGENTS.md) asserting the "cannot do full-screen mode" notice. I verified that path manually and it is correct, so this is coverage and comment accuracy, not a defect.

2. `tui.c:28-40` — the probe's `setupterm()` allocates a `TERMINAL` that `initscr()` then replaces, leaking it once per run on the success path. `del_curterm(cur_term)` after caching would tidy it, and is safe here because the cached answer means nothing calls `tigetstr` afterwards. One-time, a few KB, process exits shortly after — genuinely optional; skip it if you'd rather not perturb the ncurses interaction.

3. `tui.h:16` — `stdio_is_terminal()` is declared here but osx.c includes neither `tui.h` nor `sst.h`, so definition and declaration are never cross-checked, exactly as with the existing `getch()`. The collision reasoning forces this; just noting the new API surface inherits the gap.

(Observation, not a finding: `stdio_is_terminal()` inside `#ifndef WINDOWS` means a `/DWINDOWS` build would now fail to link rather than fail to compile. That build is already broken by curses and the stray `main.c`, and README documents `-t` as Unix-only, so nothing regresses.)

### Your two questions

**`&&` over stdout-only: right, and it is load-bearing, not merely defensible.** `printf ... | sst -t` run inside a real terminal — stdin a pipe, stdout a tty — is a natural way to script the game. I ran it in tmux: it falls back with the notice and exits 0. Under stdout-only logic that invocation would start curses with a non-tty stdin, which is the same shape as the variants you fixed. The cost of `&&` is a replay script losing panels; the cost of the alternative is a hang. Keep `&&`.

**Filing the paging keystroke as #17: agree.** It reproduces on main, lives in `pause()`/`getch()` which this branch does not touch, and the fix needs its own decision about whether the pager should consume a keystroke at all. Widening #5 to cover the two pty variants was the right call — a silently unusable screen and an exit-1-with-no-game are the same defect as the hang — but the paging bug is a different one, and bundling it would have blurred a clean fix.

### Not reviewed

macOS/BSD behavior of `setupterm`/`tigetstr` and `find_library(tinfo)` (which will simply not find a library there, correctly falling through to libncurses) — no macOS host. Both fail loudly on the first CI run if wrong.

**Approve** — for exactly this state: commit `e93b2d1` plus the modified `osx.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `sst.c`, `tests/journey.sh`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `README.md`, `sst.doc` as verified above. The probe is correct, safe before `initscr()`, and correctly cached; the three notices are each reachable and correctly routed; the linking change turns luck into a contract. The nits are optional — nit 1 is the one worth a moment's thought, since the comment currently overstates what the test covers. Fixes #5.

## The bug

Asking for `-t` where curses can't run left the player with **no game at all**. Five confirmed variants:

| situation | before |
|---|---|
| piped input | hangs (exit 124) |
| `TERM` unset | `ncurses: cannot initialize terminal type`, exit 1 |
| stdout redirected | hangs |
| real terminal, unknown `TERM` | exit 1, no game |
| real terminal, `TERM=dumb` (Emacs `M-x shell`) | one border line, input swallowed |

The last two were found during review, on real ptys. They're the same one-sentence bug — *`-t` must never leave the player without a game* — so the fix covers them rather than closing #5 with the worse variant still open.

## The fix

`initscr()` can't be asked about any of this: given a terminal it doesn't know, it prints an error and **exits**, taking the game with it. So the checks come first.

- `isatty()` on both stdin and stdout covers having no terminal. Requiring *both* is load-bearing: `printf ... | sst -t` inside a real terminal has a tty stdout but a pipe stdin, and starting curses there reproduces the original hang.
- `setupterm()` *reports* an unusable `TERM` instead of exiting, and `tigetstr("cup")` rejects terminals that can't address the cursor — which is what makes `TERM=dumb` unusable rather than merely ugly.

Each of the three reasons now says what happened and that the classic display is being used. The too-small message is deliberately short: my first wording wrapped at 60 columns, exactly the width where it appears.

`setupterm`/`tigetstr` live in `libtinfo` on some distributions, and `-lncurses` only reaches them where `libncurses.so` happens to be a linker script — verified by linking against `-l:libncurses.so.6` and getting `undefined reference to 'cbreak'`. Issue #5 turned out to be bigger than I'd written it. I'd scoped it as "hangs when piped," but ui-review argued that framing was too narrow, and it was right: on a *real* terminal an unknown `TERM` exits 1 with no game, and `TERM=dumb` — Emacs' shell buffer — draws one border line and swallows every keystroke. The key technical insight is that `initscr()` can't be asked whether it will work: given a terminal it doesn't know, it prints an error and **exits**, taking the game with it. `setupterm()` reports instead of exiting, and `tigetstr("cup")` is what distinguishes "unusable" from "merely ugly."

Two decisions I'd flag as deliberate. Requiring *both* stdin and stdout to be ttys looked over-cautious, but code review showed it's load-bearing: `printf ... | sst -t` in a real terminal has a tty stdout and a pipe stdin, and starting curses there reproduces the original hang. And the `libtinfo` link was working purely by luck — Debian's `libncurses.so` is a linker script that happens to pull it in; the verifier proved the dependency by linking around the script and getting `undefined reference to 'cbreak'`.

Both known gaps are recorded rather than buried: `tui_terminal_capable()` has no automated coverage because ctest runs under pipes, written up with concrete assertions on **#13**; and the 80x24 first-keystroke bug is **#17**, confirmed pre-existing on `main` by two independent agents.

result.output:
## Problem

When the input stream ends, the game never notices. It re-prompts forever and floods stdout, producing gigabytes in seconds.

Reproduce from the repo root — note the input deliberately stops before answering the "play again?" prompt:

```sh
printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\n' | ./build/sst | head -c 200000 | wc -c
# 200000 -- capped only by head; left alone it grows without bound
```

Earlier measurement on this code path: roughly 1.2 GB in 5 seconds.

## Why it matters

- Anyone scripting the game, redirecting input, or running it from a harness hits this instead of a clean exit.
- It is why `tests/journey.sh` needs a 1 MB output ceiling: without that guard, a regression here would fill the CI runner's disk rather than fail a test.

This is pre-existing behaviour, not a regression — it predates the TUI work.

## Where

- `sst.c:586` — `fgets(line, sizeof(line), stdin)` in `scan()`; the return value is unchecked, so EOF leaves the previous buffer contents in play and the caller simply prompts again.
- `tui.c:86-95` — `tui_readline()` has the same shape: on `wgetnstr()` returning `ERR` it zeroes the buffer, and the caller re-prompts.

## Suggested approach

Treat EOF as end of session in both input paths. The tidiest behaviour is probably to finish as if the player had quit — print the usual farewell and exit 0 — rather than exiting abruptly, so scripted play ends the same way interactive play does. Decide deliberately whether a mid-game EOF should also save/abandon state; the simplest correct thing is a clean exit.

## Acceptance criteria
=== current EOF behaviour:
  bytes in 5s (capped): 300000
=== and with -t:
  bytes in 5s (capped): 300000

input.content:
#!/bin/sh
# The input stream running out has to end the session.
#
# Without this the game never learns that no answer is coming: it
# re-prompts, reads nothing, prompts again, and floods stdout with
# gigabytes in seconds. Anyone scripting the game or driving it from a
# harness hits that instead of a clean exit, and it is the reason the
# journey test needs a byte ceiling at all.
#
# Usage: eof.sh /path/to/sst

set -u

SST="${1:-./sst}"
# Generous next to a real game's few KB, tiny next to a runaway loop,
# which reaches this in well under a second.
MAXBYTES=262144

work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sst-eof.XXXXXX")
if [ -z "${work:-}" ] || [ ! -d "$work" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: could not create a temporary directory" >&2
	exit 1
fi
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 130' INT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 143' TERM
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 129' HUP
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

run() {
	if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		timeout 30 "$@"
	else
		"$@"
	fi
}

# $1 description, $2 input, rest are the game's arguments.
check_eof() {
	what="$1"
	input="$2"
	shift 2

	out="$work/out.txt"
	rc="$work/rc.txt"
	(
		printf '%s' "$input" | run "$SST" "$@" 2>&1
		echo $? > "$rc"
	) | head -c "$MAXBYTES" > "$out"

	status=$(cat "$rc" 2>/dev/null || echo "no-status")
	bytes=$(wc -c < "$out" | tr -d ' ')

	if [ "$status" != "0" ]; then
		fail "$what: exited with status $status, want 0 (124 means it hung)"
	fi
	if [ "$bytes" -ge "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
		fail "$what: produced at least $MAXBYTES bytes -- still looping on empty input?"
	fi
	if ! grep -q "Great Bird of the Galaxy" "$out"; then
		fail "$what: did not sign off; the session should end the way quitting does"
	fi
}

# Input stops at each of the points the game waits for an answer.
check_eof "eof at the first prompt" ''
check_eof "eof during setup" 'regular
'
check_eof "eof at the command prompt" 'regular
short
novice
xyz
'
check_eof "eof after a command" 'regular
short
novice
xyz
srscan
'
# Asking to play again is its own prompt, read by a different path.
check_eof "eof at the play-again prompt" 'regular
short
novice
xyz
quit
'
# Same again in full-screen mode, which falls back to the plain
# display here but still has to notice the input ending.
check_eof "eof at the command prompt, -t" 'regular
short
novice
xyz
' -t

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'eof OK\n'

input.message:
New change to review as an expert in games and CLI games. Branch fix/eof-ends-session from main at 1b7eb70, fixing issue #6. All uncommitted: CMakeLists.txt, finish.c, osx.c, sst.c, sst.h, tui.c, tui.h, plus new tests/eof.sh.

The bug (pre-existing, predates the TUI work): when the input stream ends, the game never notices. It re-prompts forever and floods stdout — I measured 2.6 GB from an accidental unbounded run of main's binary during this work. It is also why tests/journey.sh needs a byte ceiling.

The fix:
1. sst.c — new `readinput(char *buf, int buflen)`, the single place player input is read. It routes to tui_readline or fgets, and when the stream ends it ends the session: tui_shutdown(), reset linecount so it does not page on the way out, then the usual "May the Great Bird of the Galaxy roost upon your home planet." and exit(0).
2. scan() and finish.c's readline() (used by the winner's plaque prompts) both go through it. Both previously did `buf[strlen(buf)-1]` unconditionally, which reads buf[-1] when the buffer is empty; both now guard that.
3. tui.c — tui_readline() returns int (FALSE when wgetnstr reports no input); tui.h updated.
4. osx.c — getch() checked read()'s return; at end of input it returned whatever was on the stack. Now returns '\0'. I judged this in scope because it is the same "input ran out" theme, but tell me if you think it is scope creep.
5. NEW tests/eof.sh, registered with ctest as `eof`: six cases where input stops at each point the game waits for an answer — the very first prompt, mid-setup, the command prompt, after a command, the play-again prompt (a different code path), and the command prompt under -t. Each asserts exit 0, bounded output, and that the farewell was printed.

TDD: all six cases failed before the fix (status 13 from the byte cap, output hitting the ceiling, no farewell) and pass after. The runaway is now 1288 bytes in 3 milliseconds.

Verified: 5/5 ctest; plain mode and -f mode both BYTE-IDENTICAL to main using a fixed tournament seed; the interactive TUI still plays and exits 0 under tmux; -Wall -Wextra warnings dropped 33 -> 30.

Please review the player-facing behaviour, which is the part I most want a second opinion on:
- Is printing the farewell and exiting 0 the right thing when input runs out MID-GAME? A player scripting a game that ends early gets a sign-off that reads like they quit deliberately. Alternatives would be a distinct message ("input ended"), a non-zero exit, or offering to freeze the game first. I chose the farewell for consistency with quitting; argue me out of it if you disagree.
- Is exit 0 right, or should an unexpected end of input be a failure status? Consider both a player piping a script and a harness driving the game.
- Ctrl-D during an interactive game now ends the session immediately, with no confirmation. Is that acceptable for this game, given `quit` already exists and asks nothing?
- Does the sign-off land correctly in each mode, including full-screen mode where the curses screen is torn down first?
- Anything in the six test cases that is unrealistic, or an EOF point I have missed (the freeze/thaw prompts, the deathray or self-destruct password prompts, the "Please answer with Y or N" loop, an emergency exit)?
Read-only: report findings with severity and a verdict, do not edit files.

content.text:
Issue #6 is implemented and under review. The core of it:

**`readinput()` is now the single place player input is read.** When the stream ends, it ends the session the way quitting does — tear down curses, print the farewell, exit 0. Both call sites (`scan()` and the plaque prompts in `finish.c`) previously did `buf[strlen(buf)-1]` unconditionally, which reads `buf[-1]` on an empty buffer; both are now guarded.

The result: what was unbounded output — I accidentally generated **2.6 GB** from `main`'s binary during this work — is now 1288 bytes in 3 milliseconds, ending with the farewell.

**The test came first and failed for the right reasons.** `tests/eof.sh` stops the input at each of the six points the game waits for an answer, including the play-again prompt, which is a different code path, and one run under `-t`. All six failed before the fix (byte cap hit, no farewell) and pass now.

I also fixed an adjacent gap I found while in there: `getch()` ignored `read()`'s return, so at end of input it handed back whatever was on the stack. That plus the two `fgets` checks dropped `-Wall -Wextra` warnings from 33 to 30, chipping away at #14.

Two process notes, in the interest of reporting faithfully. I briefly stashed my work and ran the *old* looping binary without a cap, which is what produced that 2.6 GB — I recovered the stash immediately and confirmed nothing was lost, then redid the comparison with a separate worktree and hard caps. And I've explicitly asked ui-review to push back on my main judgment call: whether a mid-game EOF should really print a farewell that reads like a deliberate quit, and whether exit 0 is right for a harness.
